title: Scottish Tablet
subtitle: buttery sugar confection, coarser than fudge
excerpt: Scottish tablet is a firm, grainy sugar confection made from condensed milk, butter, and sugar. It sits between fudge and hard toffee in texture: coarse and crumbly, not chewy. Makes about 50 pieces.
sourceNotes: Scottish tablet appears in 18th-century Scottish recipe collections, often called 'tablet of sugar' or 'sugar tablet', reflecting its flat, tabular shape once set. Mrs McLintock, Receipts for Cookery and Pastry-Work (1736, National Library of Scotland), gives an early tablet recipe based on sugar and cream. The condensed milk version, which gives the modern tablet its characteristic fudge-like flavour while retaining the grainy texture, became standard in the 20th century when condensed milk became a widely available storecupboard ingredient.

recipe.freezeNotes: Tablet keeps in the freezer for three months. Thaw at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tablet keeps well in an airtight tin for up to two weeks at room temperature. Separate layers with baking parchment.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar cooking stage reached at about 116°C. A small amount of the mixture dropped into cold water forms a soft, pliable ball. This is the target temperature for tablet before beating. A digital thermometer is more reliable than the cold water test.

Whole milk with water removed and sugar added, sold in tins. It gives tablet its characteristic sweet, slightly caramelised flavour and contributes to the smooth interior texture even as the outside sets grainy.

content.text: Scottish tablet is made from three things: sugar,

and then beaten until it begins to set. That beating step is what gives it its distinctive grainy, crumbly texture. Fudge is also beaten, but with more fat and sometimes cream, which keeps it smooth. Tablet has a firmer, more crystalline structure: it breaks rather than bends.

A digital thermometer is strongly recommended. The soft ball stage is 116°C, and the difference of a few degrees either way changes the texture noticeably. Too low and the tablet sets soft and sticky; too high and it sets rock-hard. The beating must start while the mixture is still hot, and stop the moment it begins to thicken and lose its shine.
Line a 20 cm x 30 cm tin with baking parchment before you start. There is no time to do it once the tablet is ready to pour.

Put {{caster-sugar}} of sugar, {{condensed-milk}} of condensed milk, {{unsalted-butter}} of butter, and {{whole-milk}} of whole milk into a large, heavy-based saucepan. Heat gently, stirring frequently, until the sugar dissolves and the butter melts. Do not let it boil until the sugar has fully dissolved.

Bring to the boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook, stirring regularly to prevent sticking, until the temperature reaches 116°C on a digital thermometer. This takes 20 to 30 minutes. The mixture will turn a deeper golden colour as it cooks.
Remove from the heat and stir in {{vanilla-extract}} of vanilla extract.

Immediately start beating the mixture vigorously with a wooden spoon or electric hand mixer. Beat for 5 to 10 minutes. The mixture will thicken, lose its gloss, and begin to turn from glossy liquid to a dull, opaque mass. It should start pulling away from the sides of the pan slightly.

Pour and scrape the mixture into the lined tin immediately when it starts to set (before it solidifies in the pan). Spread level with a spatula. Leave to cool at room temperature for 1 hour, then cut into small squares while still slightly warm. Once fully cold the tablet will be very firm and harder to cut cleanly.

items.symptom: Tablet is too soft and sticky
items.cause: Temperature not reached 116°C, or beaten for too short a time
items.fix: Use a digital thermometer to verify temperature. Beat until the mixture clearly starts to thicken and lose its shine.

items.symptom: Tablet is too hard and crunchy
items.fix: Remove from heat when the thermometer reads 116°C exactly. The temperature will continue to rise briefly by carryover heat.

items.symptom: Tablet has large gritty sugar crystals
items.cause: Sugar was not fully dissolved before boiling, or mixture was stirred vigorously while simmering
items.fix: Make sure all sugar is dissolved before the mixture boils. Once boiling, only stir occasionally to prevent sticking, not constantly.

items.symptom: Tablet sets in the pan before pouring
items.fix: Watch for the moment the mixture goes dull and starts to thicken. Pour immediately; don't wait for it to be fully stiff.

content.text: Tablet is the most distinctively Scottish confection there is. It appears at Burns Night suppers, Highland games, church fetes, and school fairs throughout Scotland. The texture, harder and grainier than fudge, is what marks it as tablet rather than its southern equivalent. Visitors to Scotland often expect fudge and get something that snaps; Scots who encounter it abroad miss that particular quality. It is emphatically homemade food: the commercial versions are widely considered inferior to what can be achieved at home with a thermometer and patience.
